prize_parts.citation: for the prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in twisted bilayer graphene, which opened the field of moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene with MacDonald, Bistritzer and Jarillo-Herrero. The round-1 exchange sharpened rather than weakened the case. Six of eight files converge on the same three names and the same structure, a quantitative prediction (flat bands at a magic angle, 2011) followed by an experimental discovery (correlated insulating and superconducting states, 2018), and no one disputes the core observation or its reproduction by independent groups. Answering the chair's first question directly: if the pairing mechanism turned out to be conventional, my support would not change, because the citation I propose claims no mechanism. It rests on the predicted band structure and the observed states, and those stand whatever the explanation of the superconductivity. From a materials perspective, the strongest evidence of maturity is that a field that could have been sunk by twist-angle disorder and sample variation instead produced the same phase-diagram features in many laboratories and in several moire platforms. I accept the chair's request to separate what is verified from what is recalled: the 2011 Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and the 2018 observations are the core of the record and are not in dispute among us; the finer priority history of earlier twisted-bilayer theory, and who among the experimental team contributed what, I am taking from recollection and the round-1 files, not from a checked source.
statement.case_against: The reservation I still take most seriously is timing. The field is about eight years old, the pairing mechanism and much of the correlated phase diagram remain unsettled, and some reported behaviour is sample-specific because of strain and twist-angle inhomogeneity. The attribution is also contestable: Yuan Cao as first author of the 2018 papers, the earlier twisted-graphene theory of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, and other moire groups are outside the three names and cannot be added under the limit. Kroll and Lindroth press the point that quantitative agreement between laboratories is weaker here than for clocks. I think that is correct as a statement about precision and not decisive as a statement about discovery, but it is a real weakness in how settled the quantitative physics is, and I would not dismiss it.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that lattice clocks are a physical test and not only an invention, that the clock agreement across institutes at the 1e-18 level is a result in itself, and that twist-angle disorder makes quantitative comparison between graphene laboratories weaker than for clocks.
responses.response: You are right that agreement between independent clocks at 1e-18 is a more stringent form of reproducibility than anything in the moire field, and I do not want to understate it. My view has shifted slightly in your favour on the discovery-versus-invention point: comparing clocks over centimetre height differences is a measurement of nature and not only engineering. I still hold that the first-order question for a physics prize is what we have learned that we did not know. For twisted bilayer graphene the answer is that a flat-band, strongly correlated and superconducting phase exists in an elemental carbon system tuned by one geometric angle, and that was unknown and unexpected in 2017. For the lattice clock the new knowledge so far is accuracy plus tests that have found nothing outside standard relativity. Both matter, but I weigh the first more heavily. On disorder, device variation is exactly why I want the citation to rest on the robust observations and not on any single phase boundary. I keep B045 as my first alternative and could be moved if the committee decides that this year should reward a completed measurement advance.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B045 for its idea-plus-realisation credit, independent reproduction in several national laboratories and consequences for constants and a redefinition of the second, while naming B038 as his first alternative and noting that ion clocks reach similar uncertainties.
responses.response: Your own point that single-ion clocks reach similar uncertainties is, for me, the most important thing in your statement, because it means the citation would have to explain what is specific to lattices, and I find that harder to state in one sentence than for B038. The many-atom magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct achievement, and the Katori and Ye credit is the cleanest on the list; I said so in round 1 and I stand by it. I also respect your candid disclosure about the Hall laboratory link, which I would treat as a reason for you to abstain on B045 if it comes to a final decision, not a reason to discount your scientific argument. On the chair's question about the redefinition of the second, I treat it as a future event and not as evidence of merit. If that redefinition occurs, I think the case for B045 strengthens considerably and I would expect it to become a leading candidate in a coming year.

responses.point: Johansson, who ranked circuit QED first in the opening and reduced its weight in round 1, discloses a possible recusal issue on B026 and B007 through the Wallenberg Centre and Chalmers colleagues, and still regards B026 as a clean, original architecture idea.
responses.response: Thank you for the disclosure, which I take as appropriate. You and I are both at Chalmers, and I should be equally clear that I do not regard that as a conflict for me on B038 or B045, and that my disagreement with you on B026 is on merit and timing, not on any relationship. I accept that the Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf idea is original and clearly delineated. My problem is the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits, which you also recognise, and the omission of Girvin from the trio. A second superconducting-circuit prize this soon would be difficult to explain as a distinct achievement. I have kept B026 as a second alternative only for the case in which the committee wants a quantum-technology prize, and with the understanding that you would need to consider your own position at a final vote.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B038 first, regards the field as mature enough to recognise despite the open mechanism, and stresses that the Bistritzer-MacDonald paper is the decisive prediction.
responses.response: We agree on the lead and on the citation structure, and I accept your argument that recognition need not wait for the mechanism. Where I am slightly more cautious than you is on the claim that the prediction alone is decisive. The 2011 paper gave the magic angle and the flat-band condition, but what made it a discovery was the 2018 experiment, and I think the citation should credit both explicitly, as my wording does, so that the prize does not read as a theory prize with an experimental footnote. I also doubt that Yuan Cao's omission and the earlier twisted-bilayer theorists can be dismissed as easily as some suggestions imply. They are why I describe the credit as defensible but contested, and I would prefer the committee to say so openly in its own discussion and not claim the allocation is uncontested.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the unresolved superconducting pairing mechanism is no obstacle, or concludes that a few more years are needed to separate robust physics from sample-dependent behaviour.

Whether the three-name set, which omits Yuan Cao, Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, and other moire groups, is the right allocation; the priority history is partly from recollection and not verified against a source.
Whether lattice clocks, if the second is redefined, would become the stronger candidate in a later year.
Whether a second superconducting-circuit prize (B026) can be seen as distinct from the 2025 prize, which affects whether it is a credible alternative at all.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B038, B045 or B026: I have no documented connection to MacDonald, Bistritzer, Jarillo-Herrero, Katori, Ye, Blais, Wallraff or Schoelkopf. My general connections (David Clarke at IBM, Chalmers and Japanese microscopy colleagues, the international microscopy federation) are not tied to any shortlisted person that I know of. My Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson has disclosed a possible issue on B026; I note that and do not treat our shared institution as a conflict for me. Kroll's disclosure on B045 and Pearce's on B016 are noted and do not change my own position.
